title: How to Pack a Carry-On for Five Days
excerpt: Five days, one carry-on, no checked bag. The exact packing formula — what to bring, what to skip, and how it all fits.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Checked bags are where trips go to get stressful: the fee, the carousel wait, the lost luggage roulette. Five days fits in a carry-on comfortably once you stop packing for imaginary scenarios. Here's the formula.

sections.heading: The core principle: 5-4-3-2-1
sections.body:
For a five-day trip, pack:

5 tops (one per day, and one of them is what you wear on the plane)

4 bottoms — no, wait. That's too many. 3 bottoms. Pants and skirts get reworn; nobody notices.

3 pairs of shoes max — one on your feet (the bulkiest), two packed. Honestly, two total is better.

2 layers (a jacket and a sweater/cardigan, or one of each depending on climate)

1 set of "nice" clothes only if the trip actually requires it

That's the skeleton. Everything else is accessories and toiletries.

sections.heading: The color strategy
sections.body: Pick two neutrals + one accent for the whole bag. Example: navy and gray neutrals, rust accent. Or black and white neutrals, olive accent. Every top must work with every bottom. This isn't about being fashionable — it's math. With 5 tops × 3 bottoms in coordinated colors, you have 15 possible outfits from 8 items. With random colors, you have 5 outfits and 3 orphans. Lay everything on the bed before it goes in the bag and check every combination. If a top only works with one bottom, it stays home.

sections.heading: What actually goes in the bag
sections.body:
Clothing

5 tops in your color scheme (mix of casual and one step up)

3 bottoms (e.g., jeans, chinos/trousers, shorts or a skirt depending on weather)

2 layers (mid-weight jacket + sweater, or blazer + cardigan)

5–6 sets of underwear and socks (these are small; don't skimp)

1 sleep set

1 swimsuit if there's any chance of water (it weighs nothing)

Shoes (worn + packed)

Wear the bulkiest pair on the plane — boots, sneakers, whatever takes space

Pack one versatile second pair (flats, loafers, sandals)

A third pair only if the trip genuinely needs it (hiking, formal event)

Toiletries (TSA 3-1-1 rule: 3.4oz containers, 1 quart bag, 1 per passenger)

Buy a set of reusable silicone travel bottles once and refill them forever — cheaper and better than travel sizes

Solid alternatives save huge space: bar shampoo, bar conditioner, solid deodorant. No liquid limits, no leaks.

Skip: full-size anything, "just in case" products, the entire skincare routine. Bring the 3 products you actually use daily.

Tech and documents

Phone charger + one multi-port plug (hotel outlets are always in the wrong place)

Passport/ID, boarding passes (phone is fine, but screenshot them — airport wifi is unreliable)

A small packable day bag or tote that doubles as your personal item

sections.heading: The packing technique
sections.body:
Rolling vs. folding is a religious debate; here's the practical answer: roll knits and casual clothes (t-shirts, jeans, sweaters — rolling saves space and prevents creases), fold structured items (button-downs, blazers — fold along the seams and place on top). Pack in this order:

Shoes along the bottom edges (stuff socks inside them — free space)

Heavy items (jeans, sweaters) on the bottom

Rolled tops filling the middle

Delicate/structured items on top

Toiletries bag in an outside pocket or right on top for security screening

Bundle cords with a rubber band or hair tie. Put a dryer sheet in the bag — five days of clothes in a small space benefit from it.

sections.heading: The "what if" audit
sections.body:
Before zipping, interrogate every "just in case" item:

"What if it rains?" — Check the forecast. If no rain is forecast, the umbrella stays. If rain is likely, bring a packable rain shell, not an umbrella (hands-free wins while traveling).

"What if there's a nice dinner?" — One versatile outfit covers this. A dark dress or a blazer over your normal clothes handles 90% of surprise dress codes.

"What if I get bored of these clothes?" — You won't. You'll be too busy traveling.

"What if I need to work out?" — Leggings/shorts + the t-shirt you're sleeping in. Or skip the workout; it's five days.

Every item must justify its space against something already packed. The bar for inclusion: "I will definitely wear/use this at least once." Not "might." Definitely.

sections.heading: Laundry: the five-day cheat code
sections.body: If your trip has any laundry access — a hotel with machines, a laundromat nearby, a sink and travel soap — you can cut clothing in half. A sink wash of tops on day 3 takes 15 minutes of active effort and turns a 5-day pack into a 3-day pack. Pack a couple of sink-stopper-friendly items (quick-dry fabrics) and a small strip of travel laundry soap, and the carry-on gets roomy.

sections.heading: The result
sections.body: A packed carry-on should close without sitting on it. If you're wrestling the zipper, remove three items — you won't miss them. The freedom of walking past baggage claim while everyone else waits is worth the discipline, every single time.
